sources.short: Frandsen et al. 2025 · BJSM · single-run spikes, 5,200 runners
sources.title: How much running is too much? Identifying high-risk running sessions
sources.byline: Frandsen et al. · British Journal of Sports Medicine · 2025
sources.studied: 5,205 adult runners followed for 18 months, with about 588,000 runs recorded on Garmin watches.
sources.found: Injuries rose when a single run was more than 10% longer than the longest run of the previous 30 days. Runs 10–30% longer had 1.64× the injury rate; runs more than twice as long had 2.28×.
sources.kordUse: No planned run is more than 10% longer than your longest run in the 30 days before it, and the Training injury projection counts any run that is.

sources.short: Nielsen et al. 2014 · JOSPT · weekly distance progression
sources.title: Excessive progression in weekly running distance and risk of running-related injuries
sources.byline: Nielsen et al. · Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy · 2014
sources.studied: 874 novice runners with GPS watches, followed for a year.
sources.found: Runners who raised their weekly distance by more than 30% had more injuries than those under 10% (hazard ratio 1.59), but the difference was not statistically significant.
sources.kordUse: Weekly miles rise at most 8% on your last full week, with a lighter week every 4th week. The Training injury projection counts it as weaker evidence than single long runs.

sources.short: Bosquet et al. 2007 · MSSE · taper meta-analysis
sources.title: Effects of tapering on performance: a meta-analysis
sources.byline: Bosquet et al. · Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise · 2007
sources.studied: 27 studies of competitive athletes, comparing how tapers were done.
sources.found: The best tapers lasted about 2 weeks and cut training volume by 41–60%, while keeping intensity and how often athletes trained.
sources.kordUse: Taper weeks cut miles step by step but keep all your runs and some marathon-pace work.

sources.title: Longer disciplined tapers improve marathon performance for recreational runners
sources.byline: Smyth & Lawlor · Frontiers in Sports and Active Living · 2021
sources.studied: The training of about 158,000 recreational marathon runners before their races.
sources.found: Strict 3-week tapers were linked to the biggest gain: a median 5 min 32 s (2.6%) faster than a minimal taper. Strict 2-week tapers came close.
sources.kordUse: Your plan tapers for 3 weeks: −17%, −35%, then −50% from your peak week.

sources.short: Daniels · Daniels' Running Formula (VDOT training paces)
sources.title: Training paces from current fitness (VDOT)
sources.byline: Jack Daniels · Daniels' Running Formula · VDOT O2
sources.studied: A coaching system that sets easy, marathon and threshold paces from a recent race or time trial.
sources.found: To improve at a safe rate, train at the paces your current fitness gives, not your goal pace, and update them as you get fitter.
sources.kordUse: Paces come from your Race times forecast, refreshed as you run. Your goal pace is used only when it is slower.

sources.short: Daniels; Hansons Marathon Method · long-run share of the week
sources.title: How long should the long run be?
sources.byline: Daniels; Hansons Marathon Method · coaching guidance
sources.found: Both keep the long run to about 25–30% of weekly mileage; other coaches allow up to about 35%.
sources.kordUse: On four run days the long run can reach about 40% of the week, so the plan adds a 5th easy run once your week passes 35 mi and you have a free day.

sources.short: Vesterinen et al. 2016 · MSSE · HRV-guided training
sources.title: Individual endurance training prescription with heart rate variability
sources.byline: Vesterinen et al. · Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise · 2016
sources.studied: 40 recreational endurance runners over 8 weeks: a fixed plan, or hard sessions only when morning HRV was in its normal range.
sources.found: The HRV-guided group did fewer moderate and hard sessions (13.2 vs 17.7) and still improved its fitness.
sources.kordUse: When recovery is low on the morning of a hard run, KORD offers an easy run instead. Nothing changes unless you choose it.

sources.short: Kiviniemi et al. 2007 · EJAP · HRV-guided training
sources.title: Endurance training guided individually by daily heart rate variability measurements
sources.byline: Kiviniemi et al. · European Journal of Applied Physiology · 2007
sources.studied: 26 moderately fit men: a fixed plan, HRV-guided training, or no training.
sources.found: Training hard only when morning HRV had not dropped improved maximal running speed and VO₂ peak.
sources.kordUse: When recovery is low on the morning of a hard run, KORD offers an easy run instead. Nothing changes unless you choose it.

sources.short: Lauersen et al. 2014 · BJSM · exercise to prevent injuries
sources.title: The effectiveness of exercise interventions to prevent sports injuries
sources.byline: Lauersen et al. · British Journal of Sports Medicine · 2014
sources.found: Strength training cut sports injuries to less than a third and nearly halved overuse injuries.
sources.kordUse: Your plan includes two optional 25-minute lower-body strength sessions a week.

sources.short: Meeusen et al. 2013 · ECSS/ACSM consensus on overreaching
sources.title: Prevention, diagnosis and treatment of the overtraining syndrome
sources.byline: Meeusen et al. · Joint consensus statement of the ECSS and ACSM · Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise · 2013
sources.studied: An expert consensus from the European College of Sport Science and the American College of Sports Medicine.
sources.found: Training must avoid too much load combined with too little recovery. No single marker reliably shows when that is happening.
sources.kordUse: A lighter week is only offered after several low-recovery mornings across HRV, resting heart rate and sleep, never after one bad reading. Nothing changes unless you choose it.

sources.short: Videbæk et al. 2015 · Sports Medicine · running injuries per 1,000 h
sources.title: Incidence of running-related injuries per 1000 h of running in different types of runners
sources.byline: Videbæk et al. · Sports Medicine · 2015 (systematic review and meta-analysis)
sources.studied: Studies reporting running injuries per hour of running, grouped by type of runner.
sources.found: Recreational runners had 7.7 running-related injuries per 1,000 hours of running (95% CI 6.9–8.7).
sources.kordUse: The base rate behind the Training injury projection for running.

sources.short: Ramskov et al. 2018 · Run Clever · intensity vs volume progression
sources.title: Run Clever: progressing running intensity or running volume (randomised trial)
sources.byline: Ramskov et al. · BMJ Open Sport & Exercise Medicine · 2018
sources.studied: Recreational runners randomised to build their training mainly by intensity or mainly by volume.
sources.found: Progressing running intensity did not injure more runners than progressing volume.
sources.kordUse: Pace and intensity are flagged in the Training injury projection but not counted in the percentage.

sources.short: Fallon et al. 2025 · Sports · injury in professional cycling
sources.title: Injury in professional road cycling, per 1,000 hours
sources.studied: Injuries among professional road cyclists in training and racing.
sources.found: In training, 1.23 injuries per 1,000 hours (95% CI 0.8–1.7).
sources.kordUse: The base rate behind the Training injury projection for cycling.

sources.short: Serafim et al. 2023 · injury incidence in resistance training
sources.title: Injury incidence in resistance training (systematic review)
sources.byline: Serafim et al. · Journal of Orthopaedic Surgery and Research · 2023
sources.studied: Studies of injuries across forms of resistance training.
sources.found: Injury incidence ranged from 0.21 to 18.9 per 1,000 hours; traditional strength training was the safest form.
sources.kordUse: The Training injury projection uses 1 injury per 1,000 hours of strength training.

sources.short: Lauersen et al. 2018 · BJSM · strength training to prevent injuries
sources.title: Strength training as superior, dose-dependent and safe prevention of acute and overuse sports injuries
sources.byline: Lauersen et al. · British Journal of Sports Medicine · 2018 (meta-analysis)
sources.studied: Randomised trials of strength training to prevent sports injuries.
sources.found: Strength training cut injuries to about a third, and each 10% more strength-training volume reduced injury risk by more than four percentage points.
sources.kordUse: More strength training never raises the Training injury projection.

sources.short: Sein et al. 2010 · BJSM · swim volume and shoulder tendinopathy
sources.title: Shoulder pain in elite swimmers: primarily due to swim-volume-induced supraspinatus tendinopathy
sources.byline: Sein et al. · British Journal of Sports Medicine · 2010
sources.studied: Elite swimmers: training volume, shoulder pain and imaging of the shoulder.
sources.found: Hours and distance swum per week were linked to supraspinatus tendinopathy. There is no per-hour injury rate.
sources.kordUse: Swimming shows load flags in the Training injury projection, but no percentage.
